title: Attention Is All You Need
summary: This paper introduces the Transformer, a novel neural network architecture for sequence transduction that relies entirely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions. The model achieves state-of-the-art BLEU scores on WMT 2014 English-to-German (28.4) and English-to-French (41.8) translation tasks, while being more parallelizable and requiring significantly less training time. The Transformer also generalizes well to English constituency parsing, outperforming previous models in both small and large data regimes. The paper details the architecture, including multi-head attention, positional encodings, and training procedures, and provides ablation studies showing the importance of various components.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.content: The paper begins by noting that recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and convolutional networks are the dominant approaches for sequence modeling, but their sequential nature precludes parallelization. The authors propose the Transformer, an architecture that eschews recurrence and relies entirely on attention to draw global dependencies. They claim it allows for significantly more parallelization and can reach state-of-the-art translation quality after training for as little as twelve hours on eight P100 GPUs.

sections.heading: Background
sections.content: The background section discusses prior work on reducing sequential computation, such as Extended Neural GPU, ByteNet, and ConvS2S, which use convolutional networks. These models have path lengths that grow with distance, making it difficult to learn long-range dependencies. The Transformer reduces this to a constant number of operations, albeit at the cost of reduced effective resolution, which is counteracted with Multi-Head Attention. The authors also note that self-attention has been used in various tasks, but the Transformer is the first transduction model relying entirely on self-attention.

sections.heading: Model Architecture
sections.content: The Transformer follows the encoder-decoder structure. The encoder is a stack of N=6 identical layers, each with a multi-head self-attention sub-layer and a position-wise feed-forward network, with residual connections and layer normalization. The decoder also has N=6 layers, with an additional sub-layer for multi-head attention over the encoder output, and masking to prevent attending to future positions. The attention mechanism is scaled dot-product attention, and multi-head attention is used to allow the model to attend to information from different representation subspaces. Positional encodings are added to the input embeddings to inject information about the order of the sequence.

sections.heading: Why Self-Attention
sections.content: This section compares self-attention layers to recurrent and convolutional layers based on three desiderata: computational complexity per layer, amount of computation that can be parallelized, and path length between long-range dependencies. Self-attention connects all positions with a constant number of sequentially executed operations, whereas recurrent layers require O(n) sequential operations. Self-attention is faster than recurrent layers when sequence length n is smaller than representation dimensionality d. The authors also note that self-attention could yield more interpretable models, as attention heads learn to perform different tasks related to syntactic and semantic structure.

sections.heading: Training
sections.content: The training section describes the data, hardware, and hyperparameters. The models were trained on WMT 2014 English-German (4.5 million sentence pairs) and English-French (36M sentences) datasets. Training was done on 8 NVIDIA P100 GPUs. The base model took 100,000 steps (12 hours), while the big model took 300,000 steps (3.5 days). The Adam optimizer was used with a custom learning rate schedule that includes warmup. Regularization techniques include residual dropout, label smoothing, and attention dropout.

sections.heading: Results
sections.content: The results section reports that the big Transformer achieves a BLEU score of 28.4 on English-to-German, outperforming all previously reported models and ensembles by over 2 BLEU. On English-to-French, it achieves a BLEU score of 41.8, establishing a new single-model state-of-the-art. The paper also presents model variations (ablation studies) showing the importance of attention heads, key dimensions, model size, and dropout. For English constituency parsing, the Transformer achieves an F1 score of 91.3 on WSJ only and 92.7 in a semi-supervised setting, outperforming most previous models.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.content: The conclusion reiterates that the Transformer is the first sequence transduction model based entirely on attention, and it can be trained significantly faster than recurrent or convolutional architectures. The authors plan to extend the Transformer to other modalities and investigate local, restricted attention mechanisms for large inputs and outputs. The code is available at https://github.com/tensorflow/tensor2tensor.

method_summary: The Transformer is an encoder-decoder architecture that uses stacked self-attention and point-wise fully connected layers. The encoder consists of N=6 identical layers, each with a multi-head self-attention sub-layer and a position-wise feed-forward network, with residual connections and layer normalization. The decoder has a similar structure but includes an additional multi-head attention sub-layer over the encoder output and uses masking to prevent attending to future positions. Attention is computed as scaled dot-product attention, and multi-head attention is used to allow the model to attend to information from different representation subspaces. Positional encodings are added to the input embeddings to inject sequence order information. The model is trained with the Adam optimizer, a custom learning rate schedule with warmup, and regularization techniques including dropout and label smoothing.
open_questions: How does the Transformer perform on tasks with very long sequences, given that self-attention has O(n^2) complexity?
Can the Transformer be extended to other modalities such as images, audio, and video?
How can the interpretability of attention heads be further leveraged for understanding model behavior?
What are the trade-offs between the number of attention heads and model performance?
How does the Transformer handle tasks with strong structural constraints, such as parsing, compared to specialized models?
